they are used effectively and efficiently to support research efforts.
This process should consider the needs of the PIs, departments, and colleges and the requirements of funding agencies.
Overall, the committee urges the university to prioritize the direct support of research faculty and activities by allocating a higher percentage of overhead funds to support these efforts.
By doing so, URI can maximize its research productivity and achieve greater success in securing external funding.
Expansion of the Committee on Research: The committee considered expanding its membership to better represent the interests and concerns of the research faculty at URI.
We regularly recruit expert researchers to help with the review of grant proposals.
We propose adding non-senators to the Research and Creative Activities Committee.
This expansion will enable the committee to serve the needs of the research community at URI.

Committee on University Research and Engagement (CURE) Charge: The Committee on University Research and Engagement (CURE), an expanded URI Research and Creative Activities Committee, is charged with representing and advocating for the research and and creative activities community at URI.
The committee shall consist of six senators and six non-senator members of the faculty who are actively engaged in research and creative activities.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development shall serve as an ex officio member of the committee.
The committee is responsible for addressing the concerns and needs of the research and creative activities community and recommending policies and practices that will support and enhance research and creative activities at URI.
Membership: The committee shall consist of six senators appointed by the President of the Faculty Senate and six members of the research faculty appointed by the Vice President for Research and Economic Development.
Members shall be selected based on their active engagement in research and creative activities and shall represent a diversity of disciplines and areas of expertise.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development shall serve as an ex officio member of the committee.

The committee shall be chaired by one of the senators appointed by the Faculty Senate President.
The committee will also work closely with the Vice President for Research and Economic Development to ensure alignment with university policies and goals related to research and creative activities.
The committee will meet at least once per semester or more often as needed to discuss matters related to research and creative activities at URI.
Adding experienced and engaged research faculty to the committee will help ensure that the voices and concerns of those actively engaged in research activities are represented and heard.
Meetings: The committee shall meet at least once per semester or more often as needed.
Meetings may be conducted in person or remotely, as determined by the committee chair.
Meetings shall be open to all members of the URI community, and minutes shall be kept and made available to the public.
Responsibilities: The committee shall have the following responsibilities: 1.
Represent and advocate for the research and creative activities at URI. 2.
Address the concerns and needs of the faculty engaged in research and creative activities. 3.

Review and evaluate the effectiveness of policies and practices related to research and creative activities. 4.
Recommend policies and practices to support and enhance URI's research and creative activities. 5.
Promote collaboration and communication among researchers and creative practitioners across disciplines and colleges. 6.
Advise the Vice President for Research and Economic Development on matters related to research and creative activities. 7.
Provide feedback and input on proposals and initiatives related to research and creative activities. 8.
Collaborate with other committees and organizations at URI to promote and support research and creative activities.

9.
Submit an annual report to the Faculty Senate summarizing the committee's activities and accomplishments over the past academic year.
Impact of University Policies on the Research Environment Some recent policies at URI have negatively impacted the faculty's research and creative activities.
One example is the drone policy which has caused many problems for faculty in their creative work.
Drones are used by faculty in a variety of ways, such as surveying, videography, construction, transportation, the design of new types of drones, software engineering for drones, and AI and drones, among others.
However, the current drone policy needs to consider the real faculty research needs and applications and has become an obstacle.
We recommend that the policy be revised to accommodate faculty needs better.
The IT department's push to take administrative control of faculty computers has caused considerable frustration, concerns, and damage to the research efforts of faculty.
In addition to the drone policy, three IT policies were implemented during the summer of 2022, which have caused chaos and havoc for faculty researchers since December 2022.

These policies were implemented without proper consultation with faculty, leading to a lack of understanding and an inability to comply with the new policies.
We support the review of the three IT policies by the Faculty Senate Committee on Technology and Infrastructure (CTI).
CTI has correctly identified some of the deficiencies and problems with those policies.
In particular, it should be noted that faculty own the intellectual property of research, creative works, and teaching materials stored on their computers.
The university may own the hardware, but they do not own the faculty’s intellectual and personal data stored on those computers.
Faculty members have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their computers, as they contain sensitive and personal information, research data, and intellectual property.
The IT policy infringes upon this right by allowing administrative access to faculty computers without just cause or consent.
Other policies that continue to be of concern and interfere with research activities include purchasing, travel, and hiring graduate students, postdocs, and faculty.

These long-standing issues require a new effort to review and revise these policies to support faculty research efforts better.
The newly proposed committee, CURE, can be central to these reviews and policy revisions.
By bringing together research faculty and administrators, URI can work towards improving policies and procedures to better support the research and creative activities of the faculty.
We recommend that the CURE committee be given the resources and authority to conduct a comprehensive review of these policies and to make recommendations for necessary revisions.

Summary of recommendations Summary of recommendations from the URI Faculty Senate Research and Creative Activities Committee (RCAC) Report for the Academic Year 2022-2023: 1.
The university needs to prioritize the direct support of research faculty and activities by allocating a higher percentage of overhead funds to support these efforts.
The policies for the overhead distribution need to be changed to provide more favorable overhead distribution to the faculty who generate it. 2.
The university needs to develop a more transparent process for indirect cost waivers and allocation of overhead funds to ensure they are used effectively and efficiently to support research efforts.
This process should consider the needs of the PIs, departments, and colleges and the requirements of funding agencies. 3.
The Committee on University Research and Engagement (CURE) should be created to better represent the interests and concerns of the research faculty at URI.
This expansion of CRCA will serve the needs of the research community at URI. 4.
The drone policy needs to be revised to accommodate faculty needs better. 5.

The three IT policies implemented during the summer of 2022 have caused chaos and havoc for faculty researchers since December 2022.
The policies need to be carefully reviewed by the Faculty Senate Committee on Technology and Infrastructure (CTI), and necessary revisions should be made. 6.
Purchasing, travel, and hiring graduate students, postdocs, and faculty policies need to be reviewed and revised to support faculty research efforts better. 7.
The newly proposed committee, CURE, should be given the resources and authority to conduct a comprehensive review of policies related to research and creative activities and make recommendations for necessary revisions.
Overall, the committee urges the university to prioritize the support of research and creative activities to maximize its research productivity and achieve greater success in securing external funding.

Conclusion The URI Faculty Senate Committee on Research and Creative Activities has been working diligently to support the research community at URI. Our efforts to review overhead funds, expand the committee, and examine university policies have been valuable in identifying areas for improvement and ensuring that researchers at URI have the support they need to be successful. We will continue to work on these issues and look forward to making further progress in the coming academic year. Respectfully submitted, Sen. Bahram Nassersharif, Chair, and FSEC Liaison Sen. Ted Walls, CHS, FSEC Liaison Committee Overview Structure The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA) consists of six faculty senators and five non-senator research-active faculty.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development (VPRED) is an ex officio (non-voting) member of the committee.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee appoints six senators and the VPRED appoints five research-active non-senators to the committee.
The CRCA comprises two subcommittees, the Competitive Grants Subcommittee and the Center Review Subcommittee.
The CRCA was restructured in 2024 to include non-senators, expanding the committee from 6 to 11 faculty members.

Charge The full committee serves as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities.
It seeks to improve the environment for research at URI in all ways possible.
The committee oversees the following areas related to research: Advocacy of Research and Creative Activities The committee is to promote a comprehensive understanding of the notion of research, creative, and scholarly work in order to enhance the well-being of all such work at URI; seek to identify all challenges that do or could hinder research, creative, and scholarly efforts at URI and provide recommendations to correct them; review and recommend policies for the management of research affairs at URI and serve as the advisory committee for the Vice President for Research and Economic Development; upon request, advise all campus groups and offices on matters relating to research, creative, and scholarly work.

Library and Open Access The committee acts as a liaison between the University Libraries (Library) and the faculty as a whole and advise the Library on matters of general faculty concern; consult with the Library faculty on long-range needs of the Library and the adequacy of budget provisions to meet those needs; serve in an advisory capacity to the Faculty Senate regarding the implementation and interpretation of the University of Rhode Island Open-Access Policy, resolving disputes concerning the interpretation and application of the policy and recommending changes of the policy to the Faculty Senate.

Competitive Grants Subcommittee The subcommittee solicits proposals from the faculty and awards, on a competitive basis, financial support for a “Faculty Development” program (using guidelines developed together with the full committee) to support faculty salary and fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment; advises the Vice President for Research and Economic Development concerning the allocation among faculty, on a competitive basis, of financial support for a “Proposal Development” program (using guidelines developed by the Vice President for Research and Economic Development in consultation with the full committee) to support faculty salary and fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment.
Center Review Subcommittee The subcommittee reviews applications for new centers and institutes to operate for an initial four-year period.
Applications approved by the CRS are presented to the Faculty Senate for a vote prior to forwarding the application to the Vice President for Research and Economic Development and the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs for final approval.

The CRS reviews applications for continuing authorization of centers and institutes every four years. 2024–25 Activities CRCA Given the expansion of the CRCA from 6 senators to include 5 faculty who are not senators, the fall semester was spent determining the goals and activities of the committee.
The spring semester was equally challenging given the impact on the changes set forth by the administration of the U.S. government on research.
Below is an overview of what was discussed and planned during this time: Fall 2024 Activities: 1.
Research Needs : The committee planned to collect data from faculty and leadership on the research-related needs and issues of the university and potentially meet with the Associate Deans of Research of colleges. 2.
Research Support for Faculty : The committee planned to focus on increasing and/or improving the support that faculty have in their research endeavors. 2.1.
VPRED Jenkins emphasized that she and her office want to support cross-college and cross-unit collaborations and would like to identify how in particular OSP can help with these efforts in addition to other priorities that the committee identify. 2.2.

It was recommended that the university provide resources for the preparation and submission of larger grant proposals, both structurally and financially.
Several faculty members have applied for NIH training grants that require a significant amount of data and tangible financial support.
This type of data collection and asks are a significant roadblock and timesink.
It was suggested that ADRs, OSP, and Office of Research could help coordinate these types of activities. 2.3.
VPRED Jenkins stated that the Office of Research can also support faculty in training and evaluation in grants that need it. 2.4.
The committee was interested in determining what non-research factors impact research productivity, such as teaching “too much” and how faculty lines are being replaced after retirements. 2.5.
The committee was interested in whether greater awareness of research support differences between Colleges could be mined for more beneficial outcomes. 3.
Setting Research Priorities : The committee wanted to determine what URI’s leadership wants to prioritize with respect to research activities so that the committee can be involved in helping to identify potential research areas. 3.1.
VPRED Jenkins was interested in helping the university to build teams around different research themes, share proposal resources, and determine what higher-level resources are needed to

get to the “next level” for research at URI.
These resources might include staff support, release time, etc. 4.
Research Priorities & Barriers : The committee planned to put together a document with potential research priorities and major barriers to research in collaboration with the Office of Research to determine how this office and OSP can better support faculty. 5.
Data Storage : Given the significant needs and concerns related to data storage, the committee discussed the university needing to prioritize providing a clear understanding of how research data is stored and a consistent procedure on data storage.
Spring 2025 Activities: 6.
Personnel Support : The first meeting of Spring 2025 was spent discussing how the CRCA can facilitate support for the multitude of personnel at URI impacted by the Executive Orders (EOs) put forth by the U.S.
President. 6.1.
It was suggested the college deans provide more information to their personnel to provide reassurance and a greater understanding of what is going on in their community. 6.2.

CRCA and the office of the VPRED hosted a Town Hall in March 2025 for research faculty and staff to provide an overview of URI’s activities related to the impact of the EOs, their involvement in legal proceedings, and to answer questions. 6.3.
The committee recommended that leadership be cognizant of the concerns of and support needed for pre-tenure/early career faculty given the potential impact of future research and potential immigration issues. 7.
F&A Freeze Concerns .
After 110 (overhead) funds were frozen, CRCA discovered that there was significant disparity in the information that was provided to faculty from their department chairs and deans.
The committee recommended that the deans be encouraged to discuss the details of the freeze with their faculty and that the higher-level communication be more comprehensive. 7.1.
In the CRCA meeting after the 110 fund freeze, the VPRED realized that the perception of the fund freeze was much more negative than they realized and recommended that the committee continue to provide feedback to leadership. 8.

F&A Review Committee : The CRCA met an additional time as the F&A review committee with additional designees to review F&A expenditures for FY24 and make recommendations related to F&A distribution and spending (see F&A Review Committee Report ). 9.
Fall 2024 Activities : The activities discussed and planned in Fall 2024 were put on hold to allow for CRCA to be involved in mitigating the impact of EOs on research at URI.

Matt Wei, GSO Committee Overview Structure The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA) consists of six faculty senators and five non-senator research-active faculty.
The Vice President for Research and Economic Development (VPRED) is an ex officio (non-voting) member of the committee.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee appoints six senators and the VPRED appoints five research-active non-senators to the committee.
The CRCA also comprises a subcommittee, the Competitive Grants Subcommittee.
The CRCA was restructured in 2024 to include non- senators, expanding the committee from 6 to 11 faculty members.
Charge The full committee serves as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities.

It seeks to improve the environment for research at URI in all ways possible.
The committee oversees the following areas related to research: Advocacy of Research and Creative Activities The committee is to promote a comprehensive understanding of the notion of research, creative, and scholarly work in order to enhance the well-being of all such work at URI; seek to identify all challenges that do or could hinder research, creative, and scholarly efforts at URI and provide recommendations to correct them; review and recommend policies for the management of research affairs at URI and serve as the advisory committee for the Vice President for Research and Economic Development; upon request, advise all campus groups and offices on matters relating to research, creative, and scholarly work.

Library and Open Access The committee acts as a liaison between the University Libraries (Library) and the faculty as a whole and advise the Library on matters of general faculty concern; consult with the Library faculty on long-range needs of the Library and the adequacy of budget provisions to meet those needs; serve in an advisory capacity to the Faculty Senate regarding the implementation and interpretation of the University of Rhode Island Open-Access Policy, resolving disputes concerning the interpretation and application of the policy and recommending changes of the policy to the Faculty Senate.

Competitive Grants Subcommittee The subcommittee solicits proposals from the faculty and awards, on a competitive basis, financial support for a “Faculty Development” program (using guidelines developed together with the full committee) to support faculty salary and fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment; advises the Vice President fo r Research and Economic Development concerning the allocation among faculty, on a competitive basis , of financial support for a “Proposal Development” program (using guidelines developed by the Vice President for Research and Economic Development in consultation with the full committee) to support faculty salary and fellowships, student support, operating expenses, travel, and equipment. 2025 –26 Activities The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (CRCA) membership included 6 senators and 3 non- senators.
The committee met regularly throughout Academic Year 2025–2026 to address key issues impacting the University’s research and creative enterprise.

The committee’s work this year focused on three primary areas: (1) supporting faculty success in a shifting federal funding landscape, (2) identifying and addressing challenges facing graduate students, and (3) evaluating and redefining the committee’s role, structure, and alignment within the University.
Throughout the academic year, CRCA engaged in regular, productive exchanges with VPRED Bethany Jenkins, who provided timely and transparent updates on the evolving federal research landscape, institutional responses, and emerging challenges affecting faculty.
These discussions were both informative and collaborative, with committee members sharing on-the-ground perspectives that informed committee discussions and the institution's understanding of research-related challenges for faculty.
CRCA also contribut ed to the interview process for the next AVP of Research Development.
Below is an overview of what was discussed and planned during this period: 1.
Faculty Support in a Changing Research Environment A central theme throughout the year was the evolving federal funding landscape and its implications for faculty research productivity and evaluation.

Early in the year, the committee identified the need for clearer guidance on promotion and tenure expectations in light of funding uncertainties.
This led to discussions and initial drafting efforts to develop peer-review and evaluation guidance that accounts for structural shifts in funding availability.
During the winter, the committee engaged directly with Sue Adams, Vice Provost for Academic and Faculty Initiatives.
These conversations reinforced the need for flexibility and a more holistic approach to faculty evaluation.
The committee also explored the proposed “Achievement Relative to Opportunity” supplement, ultimately determining that existing mechanisms, particularly the applicant statement, were sufficient and more appropriate for contextualizing faculty contributions. 2.
Graduate Student Support The committee identified graduate student support as a priority area, particularly amid the rising cost-of-living concerns and housing challenges.
Discussions highlighted the intersection of financial constraints, housing availability, and the recruitment/retention of graduate students.

In December, CRCA hosted Ellen Reynolds, Vice President for Student Affairs, and Thomas Cooley, Associate Vice President for Student Affairs, to discuss graduate housing initiatives and broader financial challenges facing students.
Key takeaways included the importance of transparent communication with prospective students about the cost of living and the potential need to revisit graduate stipend structures, including budgeting practices for externally funded grants.
The committee also emphasized the importance of continued engagement with Graduate School leadership and plans to revisit these discussions in the coming academic year to further develop actionable recommendations. 3.
Committee Structure, Scope, and Strategic Alignment A portion of the committee’s work this year focused on a critical evaluation of its structure, charge, and institutional role.
Early discussions identified the need to formalize term limits for non -senator members and to more clearly define the committee’s scope, particularly regarding creative activities, intellectual property, and its interface with other university entities.

These conversations reflected a broader recognition that the current structure does not fully position CRCA to meet the evolving needs of the research enterprise.
Building on this assessment, the committee discussed potential restructuring to strengthen its impact and clarify its role in institutional governance.
Two primary models were explored: (a) a joint committee operating in formal partnership between the Faculty Senate and the Division of Research, or (b) a committee housed within the Division of Research with formal Faculty Senate representation.
Both models would more intentionally position CRCA as a strategic, bidirectional conduit for faculty input on rese arch-related issues and as a responsive advisory body to institutional leadership.
Preliminary discussions with Bethany Jenkins and the Faculty Senate Executive Committee indicated openness to advancing a restructuring proposal.
Given the significance of these changes, the committee determined that further development, stakeholder input, and alignment with Faculty Senate processes are needed.

As such, formal proposals and decisions have been intentionally deferred to the next academic year to ensure thoughtful planning and broad engagement.
For continuity and efficiency, d rafted documents developed this year will be carried forward and shared with next year’s committee, providing a foundation for continued refinement and timely progress. 4.
Competitive Grants Subcommittee See subcommittee report. 5.
Key Themes and Looking Ahead Across all areas of work, several consistent themes emerged: ● The need for adaptable faculty evaluation frameworks in response to external funding variability ● The importance of strengthening institutional support for graduate students ● The value of clear, coordinated structures connecting faculty governance and research administration ● Increasing demand for internal research support mechanisms 6.
F&A Report As part of the CRCA charge, an annual F&A report is typically included in the committee’s end-of-year report to the Faculty Senate.
However, the most recent FY25 data currently available are already approximately 11 months old, raising questions about the usefulness and timeliness of reporting those figures this spring.

In addition, changes in the University’s budget structure have limited the level of detail available for reporting.
While the business office can still provide F&A distributions and proportional research administration assessments by college, other research -related expenses are now aggregated with broader non -research operational costs, limiting the ability to provide the same level of reporting detail as in prior years.
Given both the timing and reporting limitations, the committee believes the Senate would be better served by shifting the F&A reporting

cycle to the fall, when more current and complete data are available. The committee plans to revisit this issue as part of its broader restructuring discussions in the coming academic year. Conclusion CRCA played an important role this year as a forum for identifying emerging challenges, facilitating communication between faculty and research leadership, and laying the groundwork for structural improvements. The committee is well -positioned to build on this work in the coming year, with a focus on implementing changes that strengthen the research environment and support faculty and student success.

COMMITTEE REVIEW PROCESS The committee continued the practice established by the 2022-3 committee of seeking three reviews per proposal.
This year’s committee was smaller (7 members) than in 2023-4 (10 members).
For that reason, the committee relied on other URI faculty members to contribute reviews. 33 non-committee faculty completed reviews, compared to 21 last year (see below).
Two were volunteers from the main CRCA, one was the FSEC liaison, and the remaining 30 were past awardees.
Two past awardees declined to serve as reviewers.
Each committee member reviewed 5-7 proposals, and each external reviewer reviewed two proposals.
Proposals were assigned so that at least one committee member reviewed each proposal.
The committee attempted to assign knowledgeable reviewers to each proposal while avoiding conflicts of interest.
The nature of the competition, however, means that most proposals were reviewed by faculty outside their discipline.

The committee created rankings of the proposals in each funding category based on the reviewer scores and comments, but the committee discussed the merits of each proposal, focusing particularly on proposals with variable scores and on proposals close to the funding threshold.
In situations where ratings were very similar, the committee gave preference to junior faculty.
The committee created a written summary of the deliberation for each proposal that was communicated to the PI.
We acknowledge that reviewers are likely to differ in the range of scores assigned and checked the possibility that a reviewer might give consistently “high” or “low” scores respectively.
Because the number of proposals reviewed per reviewer is low, our ability to correct for reviewer “leniency” was limited.
RECOMMENDATIONS FOR 2026 Past awardees as reviewers The continued success of the program relies on peer review.
We recommend that award letters be explicit about the requirement that awardees agree to review proposals in three subsequent years (two reviews per year) and that a check-box be added in Interfolio for awardees to acknowledge that responsibility.

Applicants must write in non-technical language The RFP contains language explaining that this is a campus-wide competition and reviewers will be non-experts.
Although most PIs appeared to appreciate this, we suggest reviewing the phrasing next year to emphasize that point.
Committee size and reviewing The reduced size of the committee this year (7 vs 10), meant that we recruited more external reviewers than last year (33 vs 21).
Assuming that submissions remain at the same level, or increase next year, we recommend that the committee be expanded in size (at least

10 members) and that past awardees should expect to serve as reviewers (as suggested above). GEC End-of-Year Report for the May 7, 2026, Faculty Senate Meeting General Education Assessment: C2 and D1 Outcomes This is a summary of the key findings and recommendations from the General Education assessment, focusing on the C2—Global Responsibilities—and D1—Integrate and Apply—outcomes.
Starting with C2: the expectation is that all students reach competency by graduation.
The outcome is designed to position students within a global framework by asking them to engage with histories, cultures, institutions, and languages, and to move beyond understanding toward identifying and analyzing responsible action in response to complex global issues.
In principle, it’s one of the most ambitious components of the GenEd program: it aims to cultivate knowledge and foster a sense of ethical responsibility and purpose within an interconnected world.
Among the most urgent ﬁndings, which is echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proﬁciency in a language other than English among our students.
This isn’t a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

What we see in the data is partial progress toward that goal.
Most students place at the level of approaching competency , with stronger performance in applying regional knowledge, understanding global systems, and reflecting on their own cultural perspective.
These are important strengths that suggest our curriculum is building foundational global awareness effectively.
However, there are consistent gaps.
Students struggle most with communicating in a language other than English, considering multiple perspectives, and—most notably—examining global responsibilities.
Even at the upper levels, where we see developmental gains, these areas remain underdeveloped.
The data suggest that students are better at knowing than at doing —that is, they can describe global issues but are less prepared to engage them critically or propose solutions.
We also note a structural limitation: only about 37% of courses participated in the C2 assessment.
That level of participation constrains how broadly we can generalize these findings.

Turning to D1: this outcome is intended to move students beyond disciplinary silos by emphasizing the interconnectedness of knowledge and its application to complex, real-world problems.
Positioned primarily at the 300- and 400-level, it assumes that students will draw on prior learning across the GenEd curriculum to synthesize ideas, transfer skills, and respond eﬀectively to new academic and professional challenges.
In

this sense, D1 represents the culminating logic of GenEds: not just the accumulation of knowledge, but its integration and use.
Here the results are stronger.
Students most often meet or approach competency, particularly in transferring skills, connecting knowledge, and engaging in integrative learning.
This is encouraging and suggests that, where integration is explicitly built into coursework, students perform well.
That said, the D1 data come with even more significant limitations.
Only 13% of courses participated, and the sample is heavily weighted toward upper-division courses, limiting representation of earlier stages in the undergraduate experience and our ability to assess developmental progression.
So, while the results are positive, they are not yet comprehensive.
Across both outcomes, student performance is closely tied to assignment design.
Where assignments are well aligned with GenEd outcomes, students demonstrate competency.
Where that alignment is unclear—or where assignments do not explicitly ask for reflection, perspective-taking, or application—student performance drops accordingly.

So, what’s next? ● First, GEC recommends clearer and more explicit guidelines for aligning assignments with GenEd outcomes, particularly in Kuali submissions. ● Second, we recommend investment in faculty development—workshops and resources that help instructors design assignments that elicit the kinds of learning we are trying to measure. ● Third, and critically, we need to find a way to increase faculty participation in assessment.
Without broader participation, we risk turning assessment into a compliance exercise rather than a meaningful tool for program improvement. ● Finally, we recommend that certain criteria be revisited—especially––and I emphasize this: language use within C2, to see how criteria are defined and implemented across disciplines, to ensure they are both rigorous and applicable.
A Key Emerging Concern: Language Proficiency Among the most urgent ﬁndings echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proﬁciency in a language other than English among our students.
This isn't a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

At a time when we position global competency, intercultural awareness, and cross-cultural communication as central institutional goals, the fact that relatively few students graduate with functional proﬁciency in another language reveals a misalignment between our stated outcomes and our curricular realities. We're asking students to demonstrate global understanding without consistently providing them the most fundamental tool required to achieve it. This raises a set of unavoidable questions for the committee and for the university: What is the role of language study within General Education? And more importantly, can we credibly claim to prepare students for global citizenship and an increasingly multilingual workforce if language proﬁciency remains peripheral to the curriculum? Without sustained and meaningful engagement in language learning, our claims of intercultural competence risk remaining aspirational rather than demonstrable. If C2 is to function as more than a conceptual framework, then we need to treat language proﬁciency as a central pathway to achieving its goals, not as an optional enrichment. Despite our stated goals of fostering global understanding and communication across cultures, relatively few students graduate with functional proficiency in another language. This disconnect raises fundamental questions about: ● The role of language study within our GenEd requirements ● Whether GenEd is adequately preparing students for global citizenship and workforce demands In short, the program is working, but unevenly. Students are learning, but not always in the ways we intend to measure. With stronger alignment, clearer expectations, and broader participation, we can close that gap.
